🌀 #Philippine Tropical Weather Update
Issued: January 15, 2026 
7:00 PM Philippine Time

TROPICAL STORM #Ada / #AdaPH / #Nokaen has winds of 65 kph and is strengthening.

AdaPH is tracking west-northwest at approximately 19 km/h, in the general direction of #Samar Island of the Philippines. However, there has been a significant and notable eastward shift in the projected track. As a result, a direct landfall over the #EasternVisayas and the #Bicol regions will NOT occur.

Despite the eastward track adjustment, hazardous impacts are still expected across the Eastern Visayas + Bicol territories, including:
* Strong tropical squalls from outer rainbands
* Coastal and island flooding
* STORM SURGE along exposed coastlines
* Strong winds potentially reaching 95-115  km/h, especially within squalls and outer bands

Impacts will  continue through Saturday, January 17, 2026.

Residents in potentially affected areas should remain alert and take necessary precautions. Continue to monitor official advisories from PAGASA, and follow the Hurricane/Typhoon/Cyclone Updates & Information  page for ongoing 24/7 coverage.

Respectfully,

Roshin

data.raw_text:
USAF LEGENDS:
General of the Air Force Henry Harley “Hap” Arnold
 
This date General of the Air Force Henry H. Arnold died of a heart ailment at Sonoma, California. He was 63 years old (US Army Image).

America’s least known five-star general, Henry Harley “Hap” Arnold commanded the largest air armada ever assembled in history. As Commanding General of the U.S. Army Air Forces during WW II, he held sway over three active wartime theaters: Europe, the Pacific, and the Mediterranean.

Raised near Philadelphia, Harley Arnold began his military career after graduating from West Point in 1907. Military Academy classmates called him “Pewt,” after a mischievous fictional character popular at that time—Pewter Purinton. After a few years of infantry service mapping remote locations in the Philippines, Arnold volunteered to join the newly established ranks of army aviators in the Signal Corps. In 1911, he earned his pilot wings at the Wright Brothers flying school in Dayton, Ohio, although he never actually flew with either of the inventors of the airplane. From that day forward, his military career entwined with the development of military aviation and aeronautical technology. 
 
As a young lieutenant, Arnold became one of the Army’s first instructor pilots at the newly established College Park aviation school. He was involved in early experiments involving expanded uses for military aircraft, set early altitude records, practiced using radios to communicate from airplanes to ground forces, and spearheaded the first deployment of an American aerial unit when the aviation school moved south to Georgia in search of better flying weather. After a near fatal flying accident, Arnold grounded himself in 1912 and did not fly again until late in 1916.
…to be continued.

data.raw_text:
In 1942, Loyce Edward Deen left his home in Oklahoma to join the U.S.
Navy. Serving as an aerial gunner aboard a TBF Avenger torpedo bomber on the aircraft carrier USS Essex, he took part in numerous Pacific operations, including the Philippines, Iwo Jima, Leyte, and others.
On November 5, 1944, during a mission over Manila Bay, his aircraft was struck by enemy anti-aircraft fire. Loyce, just 23 years old, was killed instantly. Footage shows sailors taking his fingerprints and retrieving his dog tag— yet they never remove him from his seat.
Why? The answer is both simple and profoundly moving. The aircraft, too severely damaged to be repaired, was scheduled to be committed to the sea. In an extraordinarily rare tribute for the time-especially during an era when every airplane was precious-Loyce Deen was laid to rest still strapped in the cockpit of the plane he flew. The crew gathered on deck to bid him farewell, honoring both the man and the machine that carried him through battle.
